name: Spearmint tea

card.summary: A herbal tea said to lower androgens and calm hormonal acne; one small trial studied androgens in PCOS, and none tested acne.
card.note: The human research is on androgens and hirsutism in PCOS, not on acne.

quick.overview:
Spearmint tea is an infusion of the leaves of Mentha spicata, a common culinary herb [1]. In skin-care and hormonal-acne circles it is promoted as a mild anti-androgen drink that could reduce oil and breakouts.

The human research behind the idea is a small randomized trial in women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) and excess hair growth, which examined anti-androgen effects [2]. A review of plant-derived anti-androgens discusses acne as one condition where such agents are of interest [3]. No trial in the sources reviewed tests spearmint tea on acne.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say compounds in spearmint lower circulating androgens such as testosterone, which drive sebum production. The PCOS trial title reports significant anti-androgen effects from the tea [2]; how this works and whether it reaches skin is not established in the sources reviewed.
quick.risks: Spearmint is a common food flavouring and tea ingredient [1]. The sources reviewed contain no safety data specific to regular medicinal use of the tea.

lead: Spearmint tea is made by steeping the leaves of spearmint (Mentha spicata), a perennial herb native to Europe and southern temperate Asia that is widely used as a flavouring and in teas such as Maghrebi mint tea [1].

In wellness and skin-care communities it is promoted as an anti-androgen drink for hormonal acne and for hirsutism. The research most often cited is a randomized controlled trial of spearmint herbal tea in women with PCOS, reported in 2010 in Phytotherapy Research, whose title states significant anti-androgen effects [2]. That paper itself notes that it set out to test whether lowering androgens translates to clinical improvement in hirsutism, a question earlier work had not addressed [2].

A 2012 review of plant-derived anti-androgens lists acne alongside PCOS, hirsutism and prostate conditions as areas where reducing androgen activity matters, and discusses the growing recognition of plant-based options [3]. No human trial in the sources reviewed tests spearmint tea for acne.

paras: Spearmint leaves are steeped in hot water to make tea; the herb's main aroma compound is carvone, and the leaves and oil are also used in food, toothpaste and confectionery [1].

Advocates of the tea say a daily cup or two can lower androgens and thereby reduce oily skin, hormonal acne and unwanted facial hair. The idea rests on the PCOS trial and on a broader literature on plant anti-androgens [2][3].

The 2010 trial was a two-centre, 30-day randomized controlled study in women with PCOS-related hirsutism, built on earlier research from Turkey suggesting anti-androgenic properties of spearmint tea [2]. A review of plant-derived anti-androgens describes the use of anti-androgen medicines in PCOS, hirsutism, acne and other conditions and surveys plant-derived alternatives [3]. A 2026 review in Clinics in Dermatology covers dietary beverages and skin health for dermatologists [4]. Other spearmint studies found in searches covered unrelated topics, such as knee osteoarthritis symptoms and antimutagenic activity in bacterial assays [5][6].

No studies found on spearmint tea for acne. The closest human evidence is a 30-day randomized controlled trial in women with PCOS-related hirsutism that assessed anti-androgen effects [2]. Spearmint tea has also been studied in knee osteoarthritis in a randomized double-blind trial of 62 participants over 16 weeks, which is unrelated to appearance [5].

timeline.event: A randomized controlled trial of spearmint tea in women with PCOS reports anti-androgen effects [2].
A review of plant-derived anti-androgens is published [3].

lore.intro: Spearmint tea circulates in hormonal-acne and skin-care discussions as a food-based anti-androgen; the sources reviewed contain no forum threads on it, so the claims below come from how the research is typically cited [2][3].

claims.believers: Proponents point to the PCOS trial, whose title reports significant anti-androgen effects from drinking the tea [2].
claims.experts: The trial was small and short (30 days), and it concerns women with PCOS; reviews of plant anti-androgens treat the area as emerging [2][3].

claims.believers: Advocates reason that lower androgens should mean less sebum and fewer breakouts, extending the PCOS findings to acne [3].
claims.experts: No published trial in the sources reviewed has tested spearmint tea on acne.
